analysis.one_liner: Cuts patent delay tactics that keep cheaper generic drugs off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; after its April 2019 referral it sat in the Senate health committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug maker sues a generic company over a patent, FDA approval of the generic is automatically frozen for up to 30 months — a delay that can keep a cheaper copy off the market. The bill would limit that automatic freeze to lawsuits over patents on the drug compound itself, not patents on versions, coatings, or uses that critics say are filed to extend monopolies (a practice called 'evergreening'). It would also require FDA to strike patents from its official list once the Patent Office cancels them.
analysis.who_benefits: People who take brand-name prescription drugs, because faster generic competition generally brings prices down; generic drug makers also benefit from fewer automatic approval delays.

how_it_helps.text: The automatic 30-month stay on generic approval would apply only when the brand-name maker sues over a patent claiming the drug substance itself, not patents on formulation, delivery, or method of use [S2] [S3].

When the Patent Trial and Appeal Board cancels a drug patent claim and that cancellation survives appeal, the brand-name holder must notify FDA and the patent must be struck from the Orange Book list, so it can no longer be used to delay generic approval [S3].
The bill preserves the 180-day exclusivity period for the first generic applicant even when a patent is later struck from the list, protecting the timing of the first generic launch [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, whose patents on formulations and uses would no longer automatically freeze generic approval and whose invalidated patents could no longer be listed against generics.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and patent holders

drawbacks.text: Weakening the automatic stay reduces the leverage brand-name makers have to defend valid patents on improved formulations or new uses, which some argue could modestly reduce incentives for incremental drug innovation [S2] [S3].
A generic could launch while litigation over a non-compound patent is still pending, meaning a court could later find infringement after the cheaper drug has already reached patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — faster access to cheaper generics — is real and well-aimed at a documented delay mechanism, and the bill protects first-generic exclusivity so the incentive to challenge bad patents survives. The cost falls on a concentrated industry, with the main honest tradeoff being somewhat weaker protection for incremental innovations; on balance a targeted, moderate reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Cassidy (R-LA), joined by Senator Dick Durbin (D-IL), introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action was the April 11, 2019 committee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: the patent-delay mechanisms the bill targeted remain in place, and generic competition continues to be delayed by lawsuits over non-compound patents. Patients paying those prices are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit the 30-month automatic stay on generic drug approvals

for.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined Cassidy in introducing the bill in the Senate

against.role: Chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor joined by the Democratic whip — and its seven cosponsors split five Democrats and two Republicans, so its death in committee was not a partisan vote but the absence of any vote at all.

industries.note: The bill would cut off their automatic 30-month freeze on generic competitors whenever they sued over a formulation or use patent, and would force invalidated patents off the FDA's Orange Book list — removing tools that extend monopoly pricing. Faster generics mean lower prices for patients, so the industry's interest ran against the public's here.
Fewer automatic approval delays and a protected first-filer exclusivity period make it easier and more predictable to launch cheaper copies, which is also when patients save money.
